clue.text: Quite a way from Penelope Mortimer

definitions.meaning: a long way off, far in space
the title of a 1974 novel by the English writer Penelope Mortimer

explanation.surface: Someone is said to live a good way off from the novelist Penelope Mortimer.
explanation.definitionFit: A remote journey covers a great stretch, and Mortimer's novel of that name is a work by her.

clue.text: Sheltered side of autobiographical writer and novelist

parts.note: Laurie Lee, author of the memoir Cider with Rosie
Mrs Humphry Ward, Victorian author of Robert Elsmere

explanation.surface: A writer of memoirs and a novelist find a sheltered corner.
explanation.walkthrough: Laurie Lee wrote the autobiographical Cider with Rosie; Mrs Humphry Ward was a popular Victorian novelist.
explanation.definitionFit: The side away from the wind is the protected flank, in sailing terms.

clue.text: Like old shipwright in coach, perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps signals that the letters might be put another way

explanation.surface: An old boatbuilder rides in a coach, maybe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges IN COACH. The old shipwright is Noah, who built the ark.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means relating to Noah, the builder of the ark.

clue.text: Zip city car manufacturer in novel circus stances, later seen

definitions.text: Zip city car manufacturer in novel circus stances, later seen

parts.words: Zip city car manufacturer in novel circus stances, later seen
parts.note: Sinclair Lewis's novel about a motor magnate from Zenith, the Zip City, who retires and is seen in new circumstances abroad

explanation.surface: A carmaker from a booming city finds himself in strange new circumstances.
explanation.walkthrough: 'circus stances' is a misreading of 'circumstances'. Zenith, the Zip City of Babbitt, is home to Sinclair Lewis's carmaker Sam, who sells up and travels to Europe in the 1929 novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Sinclair Lewis's 1929 novel, named for its motor-magnate hero from Zenith, follows him in his retirement abroad.

clue.text: Fay Weldon heroine has child with first-class return

parts.note: a son is a child

indicators.note: return means the word for first-class is read backwards

parts.note: A1 means first-class, written AI

explanation.surface: A heroine of Fay Weldon's has a baby and comes back in style.
explanation.walkthrough: 'return' turns first-class backwards; A1 is written with the letter I for the figure one.
explanation.definitionFit: Sonia is one of the women in Fay Weldon's novel Down Among the Women.

clue.text: Ruins of new part in Rubens's adopted city

indicators.note: ruins of says the words are wrecked and their letters rebuilt

explanation.surface: Some new building lies in ruins in the city where Rubens lived.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ruins of' rearranges NEW PART. Rubens settled and worked in this Flemish city.
explanation.definitionFit: Rubens, born in Germany, made the Flemish port his home and workplace.

clue.text: Sculptor whose name was welcome in Italy

definitions.text: Sculptor whose name was welcome in Italy

parts.words: Sculptor whose name was welcome in Italy
parts.note: the Renaissance goldsmith and sculptor's first name, Benvenuto, is Italian for welcome

explanation.surface: An artist whose name was greeted warmly in Italy.
explanation.walkthrough: The sculptor of the Perseus in Florence was christened Benvenuto, Italian for 'welcome', so his name was literally welcome.
explanation.definitionFit: Benvenuto Cellini was a Florentine goldsmith and sculptor of the sixteenth century.

clue.text: "U" sage of linguistic usage

parts.note: the English novelist whose 1955 essay popularised 'U and non-U', upper-class and other speech; 'U sage' also reads as usage

explanation.surface: An authority on correct word use.
explanation.walkthrough: 'U' meant upper-class English usage; the novelist's essay made the label famous, and 'U sage' sounds like 'usage'.
explanation.definitionFit: The writer of The Pursuit of Love championed the U and non-U distinctions in class speech.

clue.text: Real bad errors by theologian

indicators.note: errors are things gone wrong, so the letters of the two words before are jumbled

explanation.surface: A theologian commits some really bad mistakes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'errors' tells you to rearrange REAL BAD. Peter Abelard was the twelfth-century French theologian famous for his love affair with Heloise.
explanation.definitionFit: Abelard was a medieval French scholar of divinity and philosophy.

clue.text: Some Lawrence versus with a sting

definitions.text: Some Lawrence versus with a sting

parts.words: Some Lawrence versus with a sting
parts.note: a 1930 collection of short barbed poems by D. H. Lawrence is named after stinging weeds

explanation.surface: Some of D. H. Lawrence's verse has a sharp satirical bite.
explanation.walkthrough: The page reads 'versus', a misreading of 'verses'. Lawrence's late book of satirical poems takes its title from the plant that stings, so the verses sting too.
explanation.definitionFit: Lawrence titled his 1930 book of barbed poems after the stinging weed.

clue.text: Early Bloch-buster — not exactly meteoric

definitions.meaning: an early novel by Robert Bloch, author of Psycho
a streak in the night sky, loosely a meteor

explanation.surface: An early hit by Robert Bloch was hardly a rapid success.
explanation.definitionFit: Robert Bloch's 1958 crime novel bore this title, and a falling streak of light in the sky is popularly a meteor.

clue.text: Poet gives credit to a dramatist

parts.note: CR is the usual accounting abbreviation for credit
George Bernard Shaw, the Irish playwright

explanation.surface: A poet pays tribute to a playwright.
explanation.walkthrough: Richard Crashaw was a seventeenth-century English metaphysical poet.
explanation.definitionFit: Crashaw was a seventeenth-century religious versifier.

clue.text: Jamesian prince recalls one Florentine navigator

definitions.meaning: the Italian prince who marries Maggie Verver in Henry James's novel The Golden Bowl
the first name of Vespucci, the explorer from Florence after whom America is named

explanation.surface: A prince from a Henry James novel brings to mind a famous Florentine explorer.
explanation.definitionFit: Henry James named the prince of The Golden Bowl after the Florence-born explorer Vespucci, whose first name it is.

clue.text: Doctor recalls nearly all Florentine bankers

indicators.note: nearly all of a word means it loses its final letter

parts.note: the Medici were the banking family who ruled Renaissance Florence

explanation.surface: A physician remembers most of the great banking family of Florence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nearly all' drops the last letter of MEDICI. 'recalls' just joins definition and wordplay, echoing the clue before.
explanation.definitionFit: A medic is an informal name for a physician.

clue.text: Pen Portia used to assign again

indicators.note: the letters of the two words are used to make something new, a reworking of their order

explanation.surface: Shakespeare's Portia, a pen-name, is drafted in to give someone a post once more.
explanation.walkthrough: 'used' tells you to rearrange the letters of PEN PORTIA.
explanation.definitionFit: To give someone a post or role a second time is to name them to it afresh.

clue.text: Whodunit writer partly recalling Hamlet

indicators.note: partly says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A detective novelist half remembers Shakespeare's Hamlet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'partly' points to a run inside 'recalling Hamlet'. Margery Allingham created the detective Albert Campion.
explanation.definitionFit: Margery Allingham was a Golden Age detective novelist.

clue.text: "The —— procession air which . . is given to marriage at the outset" (Jane Welsh Carlyle)

definitions.text: "The —— procession air which . . is given to marriage at the outset" (Jane Welsh Carlyle)

parts.words: "The —— procession air which . . is given to marriage at the outset" (Jane Welsh Carlyle)
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation from the letters of Jane Welsh Carlyle; the missing word describes a victorious parade

explanation.surface: Jane Welsh Carlyle complains of the celebratory pomp with which a marriage begins.
explanation.walkthrough: The gap takes the adjective for a victory parade, as in a Roman general's triumph.
explanation.definitionFit: A victory procession, like a Roman general's triumph, is a celebratory parade.

clue.text: Essential quality of Hopkins

parts.note: the poet Gerard Manley Hopkins coined a word for the inner individual essence of a thing

explanation.surface: What lies at the heart of Hopkins's poetry.
explanation.walkthrough: Gerard Manley Hopkins coined the term for the unique inner form of each thing in nature.
explanation.definitionFit: Hopkins's coinage names the distinctive inner nature of a thing, its essence.

clue.text: Ancient river renamed, in a way

indicators.note: in a way says the letters are put into a different form or manner

explanation.surface: An old river has been given a new name, after a fashion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in a way' rearranges RENAMED. The Maeander, a winding river in Asia Minor, gave its name to wandering in general.
explanation.definitionFit: The Maeander was a twisting river of ancient Asia Minor whose name became the word for winding.

clue.text: Small state writer is mature

parts.note: RI is Rhode Island, the smallest US state
a pen is a writing implement

explanation.surface: A writer from a small state has reached maturity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is' links wordplay to the definition; 'mature' is the verb, to grow ready.
explanation.definitionFit: To ripen is to grow fully developed, as fruit does.

clue.text: Narration of solo performance

definitions.meaning: a telling or account of events
a concert given by one performer

explanation.surface: The story of a one-man show.
explanation.definitionFit: A telling of facts is an account, and a concert by one musician is likewise named.

clue.text: Part Spanish praise and my support for great astronomer

parts.note: ole is the Spanish cry of approval

explanation.surface: A bit of Spanish cheering and my backing go to a great stargazer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'support for' only links, though in a down clue it also hints that the pieces stack up as written.
explanation.definitionFit: Ptolemy of Alexandria put Earth at the centre of the universe in his treatise.

clue.text: Nothing agents change in play

parts.note: O, the figure zero, means nothing

indicators.note: change tells you the letters of the word agents swap places

explanation.surface: Theatrical agents make no changes to a play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'change' rearranges the agents' letters; 'in play' means acting on the boards, not a game.
explanation.definitionFit: Being in a play means appearing before the audience in the theatre.

clue.text: Tragicomedy, for example, God willing (and the Victoria and Albert)

parts.note: DV abbreviates the Latin Deo volente, God willing
the V and A, the London museum of decorative arts

explanation.surface: A tragicomedy, with luck, might be staged at the Victoria and Albert Museum.
explanation.walkthrough: A dvandva is a Sanskrit term for a compound whose two parts are equal partners, as tragedy and comedy are in tragicomedy. The V and A is London's Victoria and Albert Museum, and the parenthesis wittily is such a compound too.
explanation.definitionFit: A dvandva joins two equal words into one, and tragicomedy is a coordinate compound of that kind.

clue.text: Goddess holds approximate arrival time for courtesan

indicators.note: holds says one piece grips another inside it

parts.note: Hera, queen of the Greek gods
ETA is estimated time of arrival

explanation.surface: A goddess keeps track of when a courtesan is due.
explanation.walkthrough: 'holds' puts the arrival-time abbreviation inside the goddess. A hetaera was a cultivated paid companion in ancient Greece.
explanation.definitionFit: In ancient Greece a hetaera was an educated paid companion to men.
